text_fidelity_a:
Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google I ordered the 'Geeni, Sentry Floodlight Security Camera with Motion Sensor, Intruder Alarm and Audio Video Recording' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I have had this camera for a while now and finally got it installed a couple of weeks ago and I am ready to share my thoughts and experience so far. This camera requires hard wiring which is why it took so long to get it installed. In my old home it was going to require me to get an extension cord, drill through my wall in the garage and plug it in, in the garage. This was much more work than I had anticipated. Now the new home already had normal motion sensor lights installed on switches, which made this more feasible for me to install. I took one of the motion sensor lights down and had to retrofit a new mount out of a piece of wood to cover the original hole left by removing the old light. This wasn't to hard to do and the Geeni light mounted with ease. Once installed and I turned the light switch on, it was ready to set up which took some time to do. I had to reset the device several times to get the App to set it up properly which was a quite pain however.

The camera itself is very good but so far I am not happy with all the notifications that I get which seem to be false alerts. It seems that everything seems to trigger this thing with absolutely no control as to how sensitive you would like the sensor to be. This is truly my main con with this device. I ended up turning notifications off on my mobile device which kind of defeats the purpose really.

Then there is the App which has thus far been pretty buggy. It has crashed many times and it is not so easy to find the "actual" activity that it seems to detect. Of all the motion activity that it detects, I would say that only 40% of it is relative. I do have the App set to just record everything (continuous) on the 128gb SD card which makes more sense seeing as there are so many false readings.

As for the good of this Geeni device, the image quality both during daytime and nighttime recording and playback is great. There is very little lag when accessing the footage which is surprising as I have other WiFi cameras that are painfully slow to connect and playback footage. This is probably my favorite feature (when the App doesn't crash).

Overall I do like this motion sensor and think that there is absolute value to it. I am however, really hoping for a firmware update which might help with some of the issues and allow you to adjust the sensitivity of the motion detection. Also it would be nice to have an easier way to track down and view "actual" activity rather than having to try and find that exact moment of capture. It seems to just tag a portion of footage, and you need to watch several minutes before you can find what it detected. You are also able to save the footage via the App, but doing so can take several days for it to show up on your mobile device which is another downside to this device.

I hope that this was helpful.
text_fidelity_b: Geeni Sentry Wi-Fi Wireless Smart Floodlight Security Camera, 2-Way Audio, Motion Sensor Alarm, Audio Video Recording, Works with Alexa and Hey Google

Kindle Voyage E-reader, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Adaptive Built-in Light, PagePress Sensors, Wi-Fi It's just plain spectacular how good the Kindle Voyage is.

I'm kind of a gadget junkie. Whenever a new Kindle reader comes out, I pass on the old one and buy the new. So I'm coming from a place that has used everything from the old Kindle Keyboard through to this, my newest Kindle, the Kindle Voyage 3G.

First, screen quality. I knew it had 300 v. 221 PPI I had on my PW2, but until I saw it, couldn't believe how much of a difference it made. Now, the PW2 screen is great, but this beats it soundly. For regular reading, I don't see any reason to switch from a PW2 to a Voyage, but I'd imagine that with illustrations and such, it would make a really big difference. I can actually read at one size smaller font than I could on the PW2.

The light: Nice light, no weird shadings. My device is smoothly lit from bottom to top.

Size/Weight: It's smaller, definitely (not the screen though). Couldn't really see any difference in weight between this and the PW2, but honestly, what's an ounce either way, especially once you start sticking covers on it? It's not something I particularly care about.

Storage/Memory: I wish it were a bit bigger. Not that I have any desire to have 2,000 on my Kindle at any given time, but once you get into using about half the memory, these devices always slow down and get ornery.

Wishes/Dreams for the next e-reader: That they'd include text to voice. I doubt this will happen, but I wish it would.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Voyage E-reader, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Adaptive Built-in Light, PagePress Sensors, Wi-Fi

Mohu Leaf 50 Amplified Indoor TV Antenna, 60-Mile Range, UHF/VHF Multi-directional, Paper-Thin, 16 ft. Coaxial Cable, 15dB Amplifier with USB Cable, Reversibile, Paintable, 4K-Ready HDTV, MH-110584 After a bad experience with another flat amp antenna I purchased the leaf for just over $50 .
It picks up 19 stations in the "low country" around a lot of tall pine trees.(20 is the max number of stations in a 60 mile radius here with any antenna according to the TV manufacturer).

You can paint the ant/ cables to match the walls. Comes with push pins for walls and Velcro for wall or window if you want them.Also has a plug into TV for the amp or you can plug into the wall like I did so it isn't hampered by the surge protector.

I get ABC, CBS,NBC,FOX,THIS,3 PBS stations, 3 Christian channels,a Spanish channel, WE,GET,MY,BOUNCE,YOU TOO, one music video channel and one other. The reception on all (but 2) is exceptionally strong with no blips in power even if you cannot put it in a window. I have mine hanging behind my curtain and most channels get 90-100% station strength almost constantly when 35%, even 30% will give you the station clear enough to watch a program with very few "blips" in reception.

I am enjoying not adjusting the Rabbit ear antenna (when I watched certain channels) even though it worked *good* enough for the money.

If you had another antenna before that only picked up 5-13 channels (for exp.) and you switch to a more powerful one like this, remember to unplug your TV a good minute before re- auto programming ( I forgot at first myself) as some TVs seem to "remember" how many it gets and stops at that number.

No need for an ugly outside antenna with this one.

When I use my hair dryer or turn on another "power draw", it doesnt get the interference the previous amplified antenna had, so probably uses less electricity, yet pulls in more stations.
I'm very happy with it. I get more channels than my basic cable had that I enjoy watching also.
text_fidelity_b: Mohu Leaf 50 Amplified Indoor TV Antenna, 60-Mile Range, UHF/VHF Multi-directional, Paper-Thin, 16 ft. Coaxial Cable, 15dB Amplifier with USB Cable, Reversibile, Paintable, 4K-Ready HDTV, MH-110584

Fire Tablet with Alexa, 7" Display, 16 GB, Blue - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) This tablet was purchased to replace my 85 year old mother's Big Lots special that she used for years and which was starting to have more problems than it was worth. The biggest problem my mother had was adjusting to the wide-screen 16:9 format of the Fire tablet compared to the old fashioned 4:3 format of her old tablet. This also had a faster processor with two more cores and four more megs of ram augmented by an 8gb memory card to expand storage. The blue color is quite attractive. The tablet so far runs everything she wants and I've even taught her to use the appstore to download her favorite games. The colors are sharp and clear. Video is smooth and while we watched only one half hour show so far there was no pausing or buffering.
I think the only thing I honestly dislike and it's my fault for not seeing it when this was a Prime Day special. I can forgive the tablet going out of stock and not being alerted to that fact when we placed the order. What I find somewhat insulting is this is the ONLY Fire tabled that comes with a limited 90 day warranty while every other Fire tablet has a minimum of one year warranty. I think there's something wrong with that. I probably would have bought this anyhow. My mom can't stand the weight of my 10" tablet (an ounce heavier than the 10" Fire) and the 8" was (and still is) available in one configuration (color, memory, special offers, etc.) which wasn't attractive and appeared to be fairly heavy.
So far so good. The tablet is functioning properly with a couple glitches here and there but every touch screen tablet and computer has similar issues. Other than what should have been a year warranty like every other Fire, Kindle, TV stick/device and Echo/tap has. That's just wrong and unfair to people buying a specific size of tablet.

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black I bought my Fitbit One after a considerable amount of research among the various "life activity trackers" on the market. As I read, my focus shifted from the features of the products themselves to the personal goals I intended to accomplish once I started moving around. Ultimately, this helped me make my final purchase.

As you may have found, I discovered that despite the choices available to the consumer, I did not find a particular fitness tracker that measured all daily activities equally well. Design philosophies and marketing strategies seem to conspire to confuse the subject further and make it difficult to match a particular product to your needs. However, many excellent reviews have been published by Amazon-reviewers as well as by online product-review writers which were very helpful.

In any event, I was looking for a decent pedometer and sleep monitor. I can't run anymore due to arthritis, but I do enjoy walking and was pretty sure that I am not moving around enough. I also suspected that sleep apnea was starting creep up on me and hoped that the sleep tracking function could share some insight into my sleep patterns. I do some biking and other exercises, but I wasn't all that concerned about accurately tracking those activities through the Fitbit. Other electronic gizmos cover those areas.

The Fitbit appealed to me because it is tiny and can be carried discretely. Pedometers tend to work fine, but can be bulky and clunky-looking. The Bluetooth syncing was also a big selling point allowing data entry to be very simple, although for some the data analysis may be too simple. As of this writing, the Moto Droid just became Bluetooth 4.0 compatible with Fitbit products. According to the website more smartphones and tablets are being added on the Android platform. The package came with a small pocket clip, an armband for sleep tracking, and a charger.

Since I picked this product up, from RadioShack incidentally, I have been very happy with it. The pedometer function is very accurate and works equally well at measuring flights of stairs, which is a very nice feature. The small size is great for pocket carry, particularly in the change pocket of a pair of jeans, and can be clipped to pants or shirts depending on your preference. I compared the Fitbit's ability to monitor sleep patterns with a sleep monitoring app on my Droid. Gross measures of restlessness were comparable for each and it seems that I sleep better than I thought.

I've worn this unit during other activities, but the accuracy of movement that it measures is questionable. The Fitbit One, at least, is probably best suited for walking. Nonetheless, with consistent wearing, overall activity can probably be deduced, but will have to be inferred from data recorded as "steps".

In sum, the Fitbit One seems to be the closest match to an activity-meter that meets my personal needs. That means measuring natural everyday movement, such as steps, stairs, and sleep, in a tiny sleek wireless package. It helps raise my awareness of non-structured daily activity and is an important tool for overall health.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit One Wireless Activity Plus Sleep Tracker, Black

Arteck Wireless Solar Keyboard Full Size Solar Recharging Keyboard for Computer/Desktop/PC/Laptop/Surface/Smart TV and Windows 10/8 / 7 / Vista/XP Built in Rechargeable Battery I selected this keyboard after doing a bit of research. I already have a solar keyboard (a Logitech) on my Windows system, and I needed a keyboard for my Linux system. I was a little hesitant to buy because I did not see any definitive information that it would work with Linux. I've had it several days, and I can say with some authority, it definitely works correctly under Linux.

The system in question is a Dell laptop running Peppermint Linux hosting a CentOS 8 VM. Most keyboards (with one notable exception) work on this system so I was hopeful it would work well, and it does. It behaves virtually identically to the Logitech keyboard and so far has given me no trouble.

Build-wise, this is a solid keyboard that should hold up to some abuse. It is sturdy and does not flex when I am typing. I like the fact that the dongle is held to the back of the keyboard magnetically so it can be transported with less concern of being misplaced when not in use.

One of the major issues I have with keyboards is that I have the hands of a gorilla and I frequently run into issues with hitting multiple keys at the same time, particularly with flat keyboards like this one. The keys are slightly bigger than average with this one, though, and hitting muliple keys simultaneously is less of a problem. This was an unexpected and welcome surprise.

Aesthetically, I love the feel of this keyboard. Most of the keys are concave and feel pleasant to the touch. Oddly, a good number of the keys on the bottom row are actually convex. While this is no issue at all, I do find it puzzling.

It is priced competitively against the Logitech too.

If I could change anything I would include some kind of indicator of how much charge this keyboard has at any given time. So far I have not run out of power, but eventually I expect to have a situation where there has not been enough light to keep it at a full charge and it would be good to know how much power it has retained.

I'm pleased with this keyboard. It works well under Linux and I don't need to replace batteries or plug it in. I really can't ask for much more than that.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4" Good crisp audio quality for phone calls. I like an on-the-ear headset instead of in-ear because cell phones have little or no sidetone.

Don't know what sidetone is? Back in the day, land line phone handsets fed the sound from the mic back into the earpiece, so a person could clearly monitor their own voice (and also hear any other sounds that the other party could hear that the mic picked up). That enabled a person to modulate their own voice (instead of screeching in order to hear themselves) and speak much more clearly. It made for a much better phone conversation experience. That feature was called sidetone.

It's a feature that cell phone designers and engineers somehow decided not to add to cell phones, or to make it so low in volume as to be nonexistent.

So until either cell phone engineers put sidetone back into cell phones or headset manufacturers start building it in as a feature, the workaround is on-ear headsets that allow you to hear your own voice while you speak.

The downside is that on-ear headsets aren't exactly convenient to carry around, and they're not inconspicuous. And they can be a bother if you're wearing a hat.

But they do give you some natural sidetone by allowing you to hear the sound of your voice. And this headset from Logitech, as I said, has some good crisp audio quality for phone calls.

Which brings up another point. Even after years of development, possibly the thing cell phones still do worst is make phone calls. The audio can still be garbled and fluttery due to digitizing and signals that fade in and out in strength. So good audio quality---in that mid-range EQ sweet spot---can make cell phone calls a lot more pleasant.

While there's a volume control on the cord, there's no answer button. That's probably a decision to keep the headset compatible with many devices.

Overall, good headset.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech 3.5 mm Analog Stereo Headset H151 with Boom Microphone - Black, 7.9"x5.7"x2.4"

text_fidelity_a:
ClearClick 4K HD Capture Box - Capture Up to 4K30 Video from Gaming Devices & HDMI Sources - No Computer Required I've been doing a lot of live event streaming and usually have OBS software running to also record. Having this device however means I don't need to record in the software and/or use it as a backup, as this will offload the recording directly to my SSD drive I have plugged into it!
I have an Atmos Ninja recorder I sometimes use as well, however it is picky about the source (if there's a splitter or adapter in the middle, it doesn't like it), whereas this seems to accept almost anything I throw at it so far. I like that. Also, the fact that it can bump all the way to 4K is pretty sweet too, as I can even use the original Sony A7S (which only recorded 1080 internally) as a full 4K recorder now! Cons are that it doesn't really have a display to tell you what's going on so you need to rely on the little LED colors to figure it out. Plugging a field monitor into the HDMI out helps, as you can see the output as well as the "rec" label on-screen.
NOTE: DO NOT use the output of this box as your stream or other devices in a chain, as the output is NOT a clean copy of the original! Imagine that this box is using your monitor/TV/output as its own screen, with its own overlays and all. One other reviewer mentioned that it appeared cropped on the output versus what his camera showed. That is acceptable with using this with a field monitor to keep tabs on what it is doing, however, if you wanted to go straight from this box to an OBS stream or projector for a wall at an event, you're going to see the overlays. It does NOT support clean HDMI out.
I intend to use it with an HDMI splitter as a backup stream, or with my A7S mark i as a 4K recorder, and for that it is perfect.
text_fidelity_b: ClearClick 4K HD Capture Box - Capture Up to 4K30 Video from Gaming Devices & HDMI Sources - No Computer Required

The case itself has an hard outer shell that feels durable and thick. I have no fears the earbuds will be well protected inside. It opens and closes easily and tightly. As much as a case can be, it’s aesthetically pleasing—a dark, slick black with a black ribbon with red stitching running down the middle (the red stitching matches the red inside). The ribbon/band does more than add a bit of style and color; it also gives it a bit more texture so it grips the surface it’s atop better.

The plastic tray inside is designed for the PoweBeats line, so the earbuds nestle snugly (but with no need to wrestle or force them in) into an indentation so they lie flat and with a mid-section to insert the connecting wires/controls into. It’s a good fit, well-designed, and I don’t feel like I’m overstressing the wires, though I wouldn’t want to leave them in that position for a long amount of time (though I tend to worry about that sort of thin more than others)

It comes with a cable. You can use any one, but you’ll want it to be very short

The port to charge the case (the battery inside the case for sticklers) is easily accessible.

An LED on the front lets you know if the case battery is getting low

Cons
I wish the port cover felt a little more durable

Mixed or Up in the Air
I haven’t had it long enough yet to check how many charges, but I’ve gotten a few without a noticeable impact on the case battery. I don’t know if their promise of a dozen-plus will bear out, but I don’t think it’ll be far off if not.

The case isn’t really tiny (You can see the dimensions above). If you’re looking for something to slip into a pocket, then this will be a con, though it will easily fit a coat pocket. It will fit cargo pockets but you’ll definitely know it’s there. On the other hand, it doesn’t take up a lot of space, it’s quite protective, and if you’re worried about losing your expensive but very small and easy to lose earbuds, putting them in a noticeable, protective case that will also charge them back up is far from the worst idea. Personally, I’m OK with the size.

As noted, the case is designed for PowerBeats, so your mileage will vary on how well it fits some other type. My other earbuds all fits in the case without an issue, just not as snugly or neatly. That isn’t a real priority for me even ignoring the fact that I have PowerBeats.

Overall, a good value for what it does I’d say.
text_fidelity_b: myCharge PowerGear Sound Protective Portable Charging Case for Wireless Earbuds Headphones | Custom Tray Compatible with Powerbeats & Removable for Other Brands | 1400 mAh / 1A Output

Jawbone Big JAMBOX Wireless Bluetooth Speaker - Graphite Hex - Retail Packaging The first thing I noticed when I opened the box was how small the Big Jambox is. It's truly portable and the name is more accurate of its sound quality. The first thing I noticed when I turned on the unit was that it talked to me and charted out the steps to pair the speaker to the iPhone 5. The second thing I noticed was the sound. The big full sound. I have truly eclectic tastes. My music collection includes rock, blues, jazz, world music from Africa, the Middle East, and the Lapland of Norway. I listen to didgeridoos from Australia, fiddles, marimbas, and jaw harps from Kyrzykstan. The quality is so good Im a bit blown away by the technology. The clarity is a wonder when listening to vocal qualities of choir ensembles, Bobbie McFerrin, , solo clarinets, and horn sections as well as my favorite twangy African and Middle Eastern instruments. The bass is great considering the speakers size. I predict I will enjoy my symphonic classical music more from now on.
But be reasonable, put it in perspective. Don't expect your Big Jambox to take the place of the power of a live stadium U2 concert or the knock-you -on-your-ass sound wall that passes through your body from a live large brass section of a jazz band orchestra, or be loud enough to overwhelm 10 or 20 loud drunk party goers. Don't be a bonehead! It flabberghasts me that anyone would criticize this speaker. If you actually listen to the sound quality of singers and instruments, or enjoy deep full sounds, spend the money (im on the cheap side) and get the Big Jambox. And dats da facts Jack.

Leather Centric 15 Inch Buffalo Leather Laptop Messenger Bag Office Briefcase College Bag Fits Upto 14 Inch This bag arrived just before we went out of town for a trip, and the timing couldn’t have been better. My wife has a 13” laptop that she loves and uses daily, and this bag was the perfect solution for carrying it on the trip. It isn’t necessarily the most fancy bag but it gets the job done and it seems to be made well. I would make one alteration to make it better, based on experiences I have had with similar bags in the past.

This is a smaller bag, not designed to hold 15.6” or larger laptops, so it is not going to help people who have “standard” laptop sizes unless this is going to be used as a book bag instead. If you need a bag that fits a laptop that is 15.6” or greater, this one will not work for you. That’s okay as it is very clearly marketed as such so it should come as no surprise. Being for smaller computers doesn’t make it useless though; it does work very well as a book bag and an organizer, so even if you need a larger one for your computer this one has its uses.

This is a leather messenger bag. The leather is a style I have heard referred to as “ruined leather” though that’s not an indicator of the quality. On the contrary, this bag is well made and I can’t find anything about it to suggest that it is made with less care and quality than the price dictates. In spite of the appearance, the materials are quality and I cannot find any blemishes or cuts, the stitching is straight and all the clasps and zippers work properly.

There are plenty of pockets to store your items and keep organized. Of course there this the main compartment which is designed to hold a computer, but there is room for books as well in the main compartment. There are zippered compartments inside the bag as well as outside, and these are good for carrying your mouse, pens and pencils, passport, maps and other important items.

The flap that covers the main compartment secures to the rest of the bag with straps that fasten with a pressure snap behind a fake decorative buckle, and this represents the one thing about this bag I do not like. If you are not careful and you catch one of the straps on something will walking, you can break the snap and damage or ruin the bag. I have had this happen with other bags using this kind of fastener. I would rather see a magnet used instead which will let go when pulled, or get rid of the decorative buckle and replace it with a real buckle which will hold regardless.

I like this bag. It is well made and it should last for years with proper care. It has room for your smaller laptop as well as books and other supplies. I don’t like the way the flap secures, mainly because if problems I have had with similar bags using similar fasteners, but for the majority of users this is a good solution that is worth consideration. It’s a little more expensive than a canvas bag, but it should last longer.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer Logitech makes the best universal remote controls and they keep introducing new models that are better and better. If you have half a dozen (or more) remote controls on your living room table and are always losing some of them or forgetting which does what, then a universal remote is for you.

The Harmony 950 appears to be mostly the same as the Harmony Elite, except without the Harmony Hub device. The Harmony Hub can be purchased separately later, though the Elite package is cheaper if you're getting it anyway. The Harmony Hub greatly expands the range and capabilities of your Harmony remote, so you should think twice before skipping it.

Logitech also sells much cheaper Harmony remotes without the touch screen. The main benefit of the touch screen is to program shortcuts to your favorite TV channels and to control more devices than the non-touch remote controls can access. If you always use your DVR or cable box's on-screen channel menu and only have a few devices, then maybe a much cheaper Harmony without the touch screen is a better value for you.

The Harmony is pretty easy to program by connecting to your PC and connecting to the Logitech website. If you have an older Harmony remote, you may be able to transfer all your device settings to this one. The buttons on the Harmony are easy to see, well spaced and give you good feedback when pressed.

Battery life is OK for a touchscreen device, but like your smartphone you will need to recharge this at least every couple of days. Most people will leave the Harmony in the recharging station most of the time, so make sure you have an electrical outlet close to where you will be using the Harmony.

If you're in the market for a universal remote, Logitech Harmony should be first on your list. The only decision you have to make is which model to buy. If you're trying to control a handful of devices (TV, cable box, DVR, stereo system, game system, DVD player), then you really have to ask yourself if the touchscreen feature is worth the big price premium. If you have a "smart home" with remote controlled lights, outlets, thermostat, etc or if your devices are spread around a large room so the IR remote has trouble connecting with them, then the Harmony Hub is a good idea.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Harmony 950 Touch IR Remote Control - Discontinued by Manufacturer

text_fidelity_a:
Kaito KA500 5-way Powered Emergency AM/FM/SW NOAA Weather Alert Radio with Solar,Dynamo Crank,Flashlight and Reading Lamp, Color Black UPDATE (03.20.14): The original review (Nov. 20,2012) is below. A couple of times, I tried to use the radio with the so called back up battery that had been more than charged, but the radio doesn't operate with it. I therefore dropped the rating from 5 stars to 3 because what's the use of having a back-up battery if it isn't going to work? The radio works fine with the AC/DC adapter that costs extra. I haven't tried the crank and have told myself that I will resort to such labor only in an emergency, which I haven't yet had. Also: You get static on the radio if your cordless phone activation is too close to the radio, but any microwave or radio wave (including flourescent lights) affect all radios, not just this one (that's the nature of transmission).

ORIGINAL REVIEW: Yes, you do have to buy the AC/DC adapter separately, but if you have a Radio Shack universal adapter, you can use that. I paid $10 for the Kaito one, which is a fair price.

I bought six of these little radios for myself, a relative, and friends. We get a good signal in both NYC and Alexandria, VA. I bought the green model from Amazon, which is fine for me because I'm not fashion conscious about most things. After purchasing them, I discovered that Acorn sells them in different colors: red, yellow, etc.

I prefer analog to digital because digital electronics has to be reset every time the power drops to zero, so the analog tuner on this radio is perfect for me. I wish the little front knobs were a little larger, but the fact that they are not totally round compensates for the lack of size, especially for people like me, who have arthritis. If you have vision problems though, you might need a magnifying glass or good glasses to read the markings along those front buttons. In summation, I like this radio and all the little connections that come with it for the cellphone or computer tablet.
text_fidelity_b: Kaito KA500 5-way Powered Emergency AM/FM/SW NOAA Weather Alert Radio with Solar,Dynamo Crank,Flashlight and Reading Lamp, Color Black

Kindle Touch 3G, Free 3G + Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers I've been using the Kindle since it first went on sale, buying every generation as it became available. My 3G KT arrived yesterday, and let me tell you, I was not impressed. Nothing worked in a way that seemed at all intuitively. It seemed awfully clunky. But I know me and knew I just get used to this version. It's a really good reader. Once you figure out how it works, it does become fairly intuitive and works well. I'm used to buttons, where they are, how hard to push, etc., so this was new for me, at least on a reader. It took very little time for it to become an extension of my hand.

If you already have the KK, you don't need this. You may like it a great deal, and think it's cool and all, but you don't need it. If you're coming from a K2, yeah, you kinda do.

Regarding not being able to use 3G to surf the web on this device. I don't care. The web on the Kindle has always been pretty awful, so less accessibility is meaningless to me. However, if it does to you and you have the KK, don't switch.

The one thing I really don't like is the fact you can no longer rotate your books to landscape or flip it upside down. When I'm in the middle of a book and running out of juice I flip it upside down with the plug on top and that's not doable with this. I'm sure that's something that will be addressed in one of their updates.

All in all, it's a really decent device, and super great looking, but lacks the spectacular awesomeness I'd decided it had without ever having actually seen it.

text_fidelity_a:
Verbatim 128GB Ergo USB 3.0 Flash Drive – Blue I wasn't expecting this to be a speed demon, it says right on the box USB2 so I knew I wasn't going to get the 150+MB/s level speeds I get with some of my thumb drives. But even for USB2, this is on the slow side. Plugging in a standard sandisk drive to my USB2 port, I'm able to pull over 40MB/s without breaking a sweat. This one? Even on a USB3 port, I'm only able to pull a bit over 18MB/s in read, and the writing is even more abysmal. That's less than half of what USB2 can pull.
For the money, this is a decent delivery platform for you to hand off large files to someone, or perhaps to play media on a USB TV or something like that. But for regular daily transfer of data, you might find this painfully slow. As you can see in the benchmark screenshot attached, it timed out for the last two write tests and never even finished.
text_fidelity_b: Verbatim 128GB Ergo USB 3.0 Flash Drive – Blue

Samsung Electronics UN49KS8000 49-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV (2016 Model) I was hesitant to buy a TV online but went to several local stores and many were out of stock since they were transitioning to 2017 models. So I decided to try Amazon on this 2016 Samsung that had many good reviews and was a good price. I was very impressed with both the TV and the delivery from Amazon.
Delivery: I was able to select which day I wanted it delivered and then was kept updated on the delivery status by Amazon. The delivery company called a few days in advance to verify a 3 hour window of time, and they did arrive that day within the window of time even though it was 10 min prior to the end of that time. They brought the TV in, removed it from the boxing, placed it on our TV stand, plugged it in and verified it was functioning. They took a picture of the functioning TV and took the old box/trash away. I was very pleased with the delivery.
The TV: It is great! Have only used the TV for four days but it has been used a lot during that timeframe. We replaced an older Samsung flatscreen (HD TV) with this one and wow, what a difference. Out of the box without any tuning whatsoever this is a great looking deep colored screen. With a few tweaks it is amazing. There were easy step-by-step onscreen setup instructions. The remote is lot better than the older large clunky devices and is a smart remote that even recognizes voice commands. I liked the concept of having just one cable to the TV which then links to a hub where you plug in other devices. Only issue I had was the TV remote could not recognize my Tivo device from my cable provider for all functions, but it did change channels and volume. I use a generic remote anyway which worked great with the new TV. The bezel is very small and the thickness of the TV is perfect for us.
Overall I was impressed with this TV and would highly recommend it, especially at the discounted price. I’ve already seen reviews of the 2017 version of this TV and some are not very favorable so I'm glad I bought this one.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Electronics UN49KS8000 49-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart LED TV (2016 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging I have a Nuvi 360. It came with a suction cup windshield mount. It also came with a steel disk with double sticky adhesive on the back. I was supposed to mount this disk somewhere on my dashboard, then use the suction cup to attach the mount. I didn't want to use the suction mount directly onto the windshield because 1) it telegraphs the presence of an expensive GPS unit, 2) it's illegal in California to attach anything to the windshield and 3) I don't think the suction cup would last very long.

Then there's the disk with the very permanent double sticky tape. The problem with almost all cars these days is there really isn't anywhere to attach the disk discreetly. Every square inch is taken with existing stuff. And who wants an ugly disk glued to the dash anyway? And what if I want to use the GPS in other vehicles? More disks?

So I settled on this "beanbag" mount with the ball mount arm.

Unfortunately, before the beanbag friction mount arrived, I was flexing the arm in the suction cup mount and noticed the suction cup's mounting bracket had already broken. I had never even attached it to anything! The mount is beautifully engineered and built...except for one area where the arm's hinge pin attaches to the suction cup's plastic hinge loops. The loops are too thin and fragile. The loops cracked and broke with hardly any hinging at all.

So now I have a quite useless suction mount but a very functional ball arm. What to do?

I drove the hinge pin out of the ball arm. Then I took two small 1" x 1" steel angle brackets and attached them to the ball arm with a 2" long, 8-32 threaded machine screw and an 8-32 wingnut. This created two "feet" for the ball arm. Then I epoxied the two bracket "feet" to the fabric (upper) side of an old 1/4" thick mousepad. Ta da. A friction pad for pennies with a ball arm attached.

Works great. Cost was virtually nothing. Doesn't slide on either of the two dashboards I've tried it on. The mousepad is flexible and conforms easily to the curving shape of the various dashboards. It doesn't weigh much but the thick mousepad has enough heft to plant the getup nicely. The grippy rubber side of the mousepad adheres nicely to the dash. Yet I can pull it down to the floor quickly and reposition it easily.

I wish I'd thought of this BEFORE I ordered this "official" friction mount to the tune of a couple of twenties.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Portable Friction Mount - Frustration Free Packaging

I was in the market for an inexpensive dual-boot Win10/Android tablet. I researched for about a week, and I am really happy with the choice I made.

What I wanted: A 8 or 10-inch tablet that I could use for web browsing and video streaming. I game and have a nice gaming laptop that I didn't want to lug around for these purposes. I wanted a decent screen that didn't look cheap. Also the ability to play Android games.

This tablet meets all my expectations. Build is solid and feels high quality. Screen is very bright and text is clear. I had no issues getting accounts set up in Android or Win 10. Android is bare bones and has just about nothing pre-installed, which I love. I would absolutely recommend this tablet, especially at this price point.

What you don't get: No video out port. There is a pro version of this tablet if you need that option. You are not doing any major Windows gaming on this. You are not going to run any extremely resource-intensive Windows apps on this. It has a mono speaker so you aren't getting a high-end audio experience with music. If these are things you need, you will have to spend at least six times as much.

text_fidelity_a:
Hercules Wireless Bluetooth Speaker (White/Green) I've been testing this speaker system with my 10" Samsung Galaxy Tab2 tablet which had no problems connecting to the speakers with and without the app from the Android store.

Appearance:
Their product description calls this 'fun, trendy and modern'. But to be honest this looks, to me, like an appliance that fell out of my grandmother's 1950's black, white and chrome art-deco kitchen. It's not unpleasant looking but I wouldn't call it modern. When I saw images of the system online I had hopes that the neon green ring around the face would light up. Sadly it doesn't. The handle is also fixed in place and doesn't retract or collapse into the body. It would have been a nice idea so you could stack or store this more easily.

Sound:
It doesn't sound bad. Especially for being just two 15 watt wide range speakers in a ported (holes to help the bass sound better) enclosure. The bass is a little flat and the high end sounds a little... hollow but it is a lot better than the speakers built into my tablet. I've tried a variety of music; jazz, pop, classical, rock, punk and everything sounded quite good. I found I had to use both the tablet's volume control as well as the speaker systems volume controls to get real volume out of the system. They operate independently of each other.

Drawbacks:
I don't normally comment on price with items received from the Vine program but at the time I'm writing this review Amazon is currently selling this item for over two hundred dollars. Maybe the Bluetooth equipment is expensive but to me that's a LOT for just two speakers in a box. I didn't pay that much for my four speaker bookshelf system or the subwoofer equipped speaker system connected to my desktop PC. Both of which have far superior sound quality.

The battery indicator light only seems to light up when the system is charging. I charged this a week ago and used it for several hours at a time but I have no idea how much charge is left in the battery.

The biggest problem I had with this speaker system was when doing anything other than playing music. I thought it would be fun to add big sound to the games I enjoy on my tablet but there's a distinct lag between doing anything and when the speaker plays the sound. I noticed it most of all in my favorite billiards simulator. You would strike a ball...and then hear it happen, even system sounds such as keyboard typing noises, a 'blip' when selecting things played a noticeable time after they happened.

The App:
I won't say much about the app here. It's completely unnecessary to operate this system with your Android device. It's just poor quality programming that appears to have been slapped together at the last minute. It also doesn't match the documentation and features such as Bass Boost which are in the instructions but don't exist in the app.

Speaking of the documentation. I opened the box and found a large booklet and for one, brief, moment I thought this item was fully documented in depth and detail... then I opened the instructions and found there's twelve pages of English instructions which are poorly written and lacking in detail. The rest of the book is comprised of numerous other languages each getting their own few pages. Ah well. Turn it on, turn it up. Enjoy the music.
text_fidelity_b: Hercules Wireless Bluetooth Speaker (White/Green)

Homvare Hard Shell Case for Over The Ear Headphones with Full Protection fits Beats Studio, Solo 3, Sony, Bose QC, JBL, Sennheiser, Skullcandy, mPow, Audio Technica, Cowin, JVC, Panasonic I wanted a simple hardshell case to attach a carabiner to and sling my noise-canceling headphones off my backpack. This did the job. It was fine, I was pleased.

Then I came back from a December trip to Helsinki and somewhere between baggage claim at DFW and my front door, the case - with my beloved headphones, a battery bank, and my Apple rapid charge block - vanished.

I was heartbroken. I filed reports. I checked with my Lyft driver. I went through my backpack and suitcase over and over and over again. I poked the bushes around my apartment building. Nothing.

Fast forward four months to today. I took the trash out and as I came back up the stairs, I saw something dark colored under the feral cat shelter on my patio. In all these months I’d never noticed it. But when I lifted the shelter, there it was. Filthy, scratched up, covered in pollen - my headphone case. I believe I knocked it under there while I was looking for my house keys.

In the last four months the DFW area has seen torrential downpours, freezing sleet, and even snowdrifts. My porch often catches the brunt of these storms. And yet when I zipped the case open, my headphones and battery bank and charging block were perfectly fine. Not so much as a dust mote on them. Everything was still fully charged and absolutely totally functional. As if they hadn’t just spent four months outdoors in Texas’ wacky winter weather under a cat hutch. Completely perfect.

And the case may be fine externally as well once I take some Clorox wipes to it.

Anyway. Good case, STUPENDOUS dang value for the cost.
text_fidelity_b: Homvare Hard Shell Case for Over The Ear Headphones with Full Protection fits Beats Studio, Solo 3, Sony, Bose QC, JBL, Sennheiser, Skullcandy, mPow, Audio Technica, Cowin, JVC, Panasonic

text_fidelity_a:
Nikon D3100 DSLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Auto Focus-S Nikkor Zoom Lens (Discontinued by Manufacturer) First, let me preface that I in NO way count myself a photog. I am just a shutter bug who has been firing frames almost non-stop since the age of 18. I learned on my dad's 'old' Nikon SLR with an f/1.2 lens. The Nikon SLRs/DSLRs I have owned are: N50, N60, N55, N80 and D50. My N50 ad N80 had the best lenses. The N60 and N55 were not as great and the D50 was a fabulous entry-level digital. The only medium format camera I own is my Holga. But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0 Comcast has repeatedly lied to me, sending me letters and alerts telling me that I need a new cable modem or my service will be seriously degraded. One time they went so far as to set a date when my service would NO longer work at all! Of course, I would never believe them without double-checking for myself, and I found out it was indeed an outright lie. Even the oldest DOCSIS versions can handle more than my 30Mbps connection. I suppose the lie was because they want me to rent their modem for $10 or more a month and relinquish control of my own network to them.

That said, it makes sense to upgrade when convenient to be sure you're future proofed. Eventually even the cheapest Internet plans will be upgraded to higher speeds. When I heard that I could register this on Comcast's network online without having to call them (and have them speak extremely condescendingly to me even though I'm a Systems Engineer), I was sold. Worth doing.

Note that just because DOCSIS 3.0 can reach speeds of 10Gbps with maxed out number of channels, this modem is 680Mbps, which will be out of date eventually, when we finally get Gigabit Ethernet to residences.

Another (of a million) thing(s) I hate about Comcast is that they by default use your AP (that they rent to you as part of a router/AP/modem combo) to create a public (virtual) wireless AP for their other customers. They say this will not affect your bandwidth, but it can affect your throughput. And it uses your electricity. And why would you want to help Comcast, when they take advantage of you any chance they can.

Point of all this is me encouraging you to get your own modem, get your own router and AP (or combo unit, although I prefer them separate) and pare down your ISP bill as much as you can. Stop giving them money.

Note that apparently if you get voice service through Comcast, you'll still need their combo modem unit of some sort. Well, cut that service from your monthly budget too. If we just had some competition, I'd cut Comcast out of my life completely.

Another thing is that if you have their modem and you need help with it, they may call it your responsibility and charge you for any "help" they provide. At least if you own your own stuff, you'll know if it's your problem or theirs.

Modem is straightforward and easy to use as any. If you ever download at high rates for days on end, it'll need cycled, but that's not the modem's fault; it just happens.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Cable Modem CM500 - Compatible with all Cable Providers incl. Xfinity, Spectrum, Cox | For Cable Plans up to 400Mbps | DOCSIS 3.0

text_fidelity_a:
Apple AirPods Max Wireless Over-Ear Headphones. Active Noise Cancelling, Transparency Mode, Spatial Audio, Digital Crown for Volume Control. Bluetooth Headphones for iPhone - Green I see people raving up and down about the perfection and wonderfulness of these headphones; I’m not as completely blown away by them as those people are. Quality of construction does seem to be excellent (although because Amazon doesn’t lower all prices at the start of Prime Day but only lowers some of them well after Prime Day has begun, I had to send back the first pair I bought and purchase another pair to get a discounted price, and the piston things for extending and compressing the size of the headphones was smoother on the first pair I had) and they’re comfortable enough to wear for extended periods, but while it may be a limitation of Bluetooth (I don’t know), I haven’t noticed myself being amazed by their bass response. No, in fact I just now watched the video for Shake It Off and listened to a couple of Lana Del Rey tracks and these headphones are definitely lacking in bass response – as in, there’s very little, and what there is gets completely lost under any midrange and high-end sounds that may be playing at the same time. They’re tinny-sounding. I have to wonder what the people are listening to with these who are praising the sound quality so enthusiastically.

On the other hand, I don’t ordinarily listen to music anymore, but only to talks and lectures; While I’m watching movies is probably the only time I’m going to really want big bass, and I watched The Revenant last night and didn’t feel like I was missing anything…

So their construction is much more solid than that of probably most other headphones on the market, they’re comfortable to wear, and there’s a nice ecosystem of accessories out there, but I personally find the sound quality quite lacking and I’m going to have to decide whether to hang onto these or return them.

Otherwise, this is well made, with sturdy looking and smoothly functioning zippers, robust strap & handle, and functional side pockets. Certainly a good product, you won't regret buying this case, other than possible regret over the price paid. Sometimes you want a switch, sometimes you don't. Sometimes you want it to light up, sometimes you don't. This one doesn't light up. If I want a switch to turn off equipment, I often want to keep it off most of the time, so I want the light to be able to see it. On the other hand, if I keep the equipment on most of the time, then I don't need extra lights being powered (no matter how insignificant).

14AWG conductors and ground mean you can get the maximum out of most household circuits (because most are 15 amp). I don't like any extension cords or strips less than that to avoid voltage drop, overloading, etc.

Love the flat plug, especially for semi-permanent installations.

Wish the cord was more white considering my trim is white, but it's close enough to not annoy me in most cases.

Still very much liking my purchase. Still rocking Merlin firmware. No issues with stability or performance.

Edit:

I have moved from the standard firmware to an open version, search for "ASUSWRT-Merlin" if interested. This has fixed my IP address issue as well as made several other improvements. The changes are too many to mention. That doesn't mean new features but bug fix's and so forth. However, if non stock firmware is not your cup of tea. ASUS rolls many of the fixs into its firmware from my understanding. So if you want to maintain more stock and less bleeding edge. Simply wait a bit longer and most of the changes will make it to you.

I am still very thrilled with my purchase.

The only thing I find meh is the antennas tend to be more floppy than I would like. However if you set it and don't get behind it monkeying around they stay just fine. I am sure many of us know the cord hell behind the entertainment center. This past go round I eliminated 90% of that and hopefully made it future proof. The only area still needing tweaking is behind my router. :(

Oh, I also turned off the smart connect feature. I was having issues with some of my iOS devices and its just easier for me to keep 3 separate SSID's and use them.
I maintain the following.
1 - 2.4 GHz for the IOT devices such as smart lights switches, older iOS devices of the kid's, etc.
1 - 5 GHz for all higher capable devices, media streaming devices so forth. Also configured as failover protection in devices that can support multiple configs and use ethernet first and wifi on failure of ethernet.
1 - 5 GHz for the wife's MacBook / iOS devices, my MacBook / iOS devices etc.

I am going to experiment using the smart connect more soon and see if the previous usage changes.

I purchased this to replace an aging Airport Extreme. I love the unit. It is easy to setup and the GUI is stable in Safari on OSX, Which I, often find other manufacturers have issues with. I had returned a competing product a week earlier as it had a security flaw. I could not be happier with my decision to spend the extra money. I generally believe you get what you pay for however, I was skeptical. So far it lives up to expectations and I think I received my moneys worth. It is a hefty sized unit. As for range, I have an older plaster walled home ( @ 1300 sq f) with metal mesh backing through out the home. Normally router signal don't play well, however the unit appears to reach all the corners of my home. I was using multiple Airport expresses as access point to fill in the holes so to speak. I have been able to turn off those units.

The only issue I had with the unit is the static IP is capped at 64 places. Additionally the GUI will take mac addresses as lower case. *Do not input the addresses using lower case.* It will prevent you from customizing the device name and the graphic. Once you remove the entry and re add it properly using upper case letters/numbers, you can easily customize the entry to your liking. This small issue is by no means a deal breaker for me. Its good points far out weigh its few issues.

I have 9 daily devices on WiFi and three TiVo receivers that connect via Ethernet or WiFi plus the land line phone. There's four Ethernet connections and two phone connections on the modem, plenty for our needs.

It's been almost three weeks and I've noticed an astonishing improvement in our initial connection and reliability. Rather than daily outages, we have had five total in three weeks and none lasted more than 15 to 20 minutes. Stability of the signal has improved and our speeds are double what they were with the arris modem - we're actually getting the high speed service we pay for. The router is also projecting the WiFi far enough that I no longer need to use a secondary extender to get WiFi by the pool and patio.

I like the Genie app with this. The ability to check channels, reboot the router if needed, and see which devices are online is very handy. I also like the clear, bright lights on the front. At a glance you know if there's a problem. Bottom line for me is that I haven't canceled our services from Suddenlink because this unit fixed 90% of our problem.

text_fidelity_a:
Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red) The Fujifilm FinePix Z90 is a great point and shoot camera. It comes in a variety of colors, but I like the bright red finish of the camera I have. The design is unique from other cameras - it resembles a wallet or envelope. To turn the camera on, you simply slide the lens cover down; this is the part of the camera that looks like an envelope flap. Some of the options are a little harder to use than other small cameras, but the available features are worth a little time to learn to use.

Besides the stylish design, I like the many innovative features of the camera. For example, it's very easy to switch from playback to camera mode with the buttons on the camera. Once in playback mode, I found the functionality to have many more options compared to other similar cameras. You can compare photos side-by-side or with the press of an on-screen button, you can display thumbnails of several photos at once.

There are too many features to describe each one in detail, but below is a summary of my favorites:
* Good picture quality for size and type of camera
* Many settings manageable by touching the screen
* Robust playback mode
* Includes lithium ion battery and charger
* Ability to take one photo without flash and immediately take same picture with flash and compare results side-by-side (Great for taking an initial photo to test lighting conditions)
* Can load photos to PC even without the included software using standard windows functionality
* In Playback mode, can go to Menu and select specific photo. Then when photos are loaded to the PC, only those selected photos will be uploaded to Facebook.
* Zoom in/out easily by touching a round button on top of the camera - easier to get to and use than the bars on other cameras that must be tapped on one end or the other to zoom in and out
* Can select a mode that allows a photo to be taken by touching the screen instead of the shutter button
* When turning the camera vertically to take a picture, the menu options are automatically displayed in a portrait mode so they are easy to read

Overall, this camera has several unique, up-to-date features that are surprising, especially for a camera at this price point. The stylish design makes it a great choice for adults or teens. Facebook and YouTube users will appreciate the technology making is easier than ever to post photos and video clips. If you're looking for a small camera with a fun design and new features, the FinePix is worth a second look.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix Z90 14 MP Digital Camera with Fujinon 5x Wide Angle Optical Zoom Lens and 3-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Red)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Keyboard, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers I had decided I did not "need" a Kindle, having tons of other gadgets for all sorts of things. Then I began to lose the vision in one eye and realized over a period of weeks that I could not read normally (or at all some days). Magazines, books, the newspaper.... heck even email was difficult to impossible some days. All my friends have Kindles, so I borrowed one for a day and fell in love. We immediately ordered the Special Offers Wi-Fi Keyboard version. I've had it about 45 days now and my quality of life has seriously improved! I can enlarge the font and change the style of the font depending on my needs at that moment and on really bad days, when my eyes are tired or refusing to focus, the voice function is amazing. The very idea that it reads aloud to me is tremendous and once you adjust to the sometimes robotic pronounciation of some words, it works like a charm. So far, all the books I've purchased have allowed the voice option.

I signed up for Audible.com about two weeks after getting the Kindle and the quality of the audio books on my Kindle is excellent. No robotic voice here - you get the narration exactly as read by the real person - it's an MP3 file I think. Additionally, getting the local newspaper every morning on my Kindle has returned to me my morning tradition of the local editorials & coffee. I do love the number of free books available as well - some are garbage, but most are pretty decent and some have been excellent books. (Loads of Sc-Fi for free too, what's not to love?) I have used the sample option for a ton of books and it's helped me decide to spend the money purchasing a novel, or not. In case you are worried about the Special Offers... they are the screensavers while the Kindle is in sleep mode and NEVER show up in your actual books. I've used a couple of them already now that I think about it.

One last thing - the Kindle in a case, fits into almost all of my handbags and has saved my sanity sitting in doctor's office waiting rooms and at the car repair shop, and I can now sit out under a tree on a pretty day with my horses again while I read a great book. This version of the Kindle will also play my own music while I'm reading. Bottom line is that the Kindle has helped me get a valuable part of my life back and this in turn has allowed me to be more rational while facing possible permanent loss of vision in one eye. Very worthwhile purchase!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Keyboard, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers

text_fidelity_a:
Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

When I use the GPS exercise mode, the results start showing big differences. On today's run, Garmin recorded 4.02 miles while Epson says 3.9 miles. That's a 3% difference which is close enough for me. Garmin says 529 calories and Epson says 955 calories. Garmin says 535 feet of elevation gain and Epson says 1142 feet. I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.
text_fidelity_b: Epson ProSense 347 GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate and Ultra Long Battery Life - Black

text_fidelity_a:
KINESIS Freestyle2 Ergonomic Keyboard w/ VIP3 Lifters for Mac (9" Separation) UPDATE 1/5/14: I'm downgrading my rating of this keyboard to three stars for one main reason: there are very sharp edges on the inside of the two sides of this split keyboard which can cut your wrists if you aren't careful. I put my mouse in between the two sides of the keyboard because that is the best position for it for me to prevent back and arm strain. Unfortunately, every time I use the mouse, my right wrist runs into the sharp edges of the inside of the right side of this split keyboard. To give you an idea how bad this sharpness is, I wear a [[ASIN:B008C27UPQ sport wristband]] to protect my wrist, and it is literally shredding from coming in contact with the knife-sharp plastic edge. I have tried putting duct tape over the sharp edge, but it won't stick to the plastic this keyboard is made of, and to add insult to injury, the tape looks awful.

Previous Review:

I recently had a bad flare-up of right arm pain from repetitive stress. I experimented to figure out which movements at my computer were hurting me the most, and I realized that reaching for the mouse was even more painful than keyboarding. As a result, I searched for keyboards here on Amazon with the potential to be divided in half, so that I could place my mouse right in front of me. That search led me to this keyboard.

This "freestyle" keyboard gives you the option to either leave the two sides hooked together and place it at a 45-degree angle on each side, or unhook the two sides totally. It is a simple procedure, no tools required, to unhook the two sides.

This product comes with instructions for putting the keyboard together from scratch, but everything came assembled except for mounting the padding that supposedly goes under your wrists--I have medium-sized hands, and the padding lands at the base of my hands, nowhere near my wrists. The padding also is not very thick, and I'm not sure why the manufacturer did not just go ahead and paste on the padding themselves--it's a hassle making sure it is totally straight before you stick it on. It can't be re-positioned if you mess up. Fortunately, I didn't mess up, and I don't have a huge need to support my wrists, so I am not downgrading my rating for that, but some consumers might want to know about it.

I really like the ability to put my mouse pad in between the two halves. This works as well as I had hoped to prevent the strain of reaching for the mouse constantly. The keys have a nice feel to them, as well. I am a touch typist, and I was very concerned at first that I would lose that ability on a strange keyboard. I have learned after multiple long days of using the keyboard that the trick is to get my fingers in the right position to begin with, such that my right pointer finger is on the J, and my left pointer finger is on the F. Even so, I currently hit false keys much more than normal. I hope that time and use will overcome this issue. I have ordered an additional one of these keyboards to hook up to my laptop so that I am always employing the same keyboarding reflexes, in order to more quickly retrain my brain.

This keyboard is certainly much more expensive than the $15-19 keyboards I've used forever, but will be well worth the price if it, as I think it will, helps prevent the excruciating pain of repetitive stress syndrome.

This keyboard is made so that the inner section can be elevated at either of two selected heights, or it can be fairly flat. This is useful for varying the position of the hands. As a physical therapist told me years ago, changing position and resting are crucial for preventing repetitive stress. I've tried all three levels, and I find the highest one the most comfortable.

Another plus of this keyboard is that I can now bilaterally employ a beneficial PT suggestion: I have for years placed a pillow under my right arm which is positioned against the arm of my [[ASIN:B000PWGZOI rolling office chair]]. This takes the strain off my arm and shoulder by bracing them. The fact that I'm using a pillow means that I am not in danger of damaging the brachial plexus nerve in the axilla (underarm), which can happen with hard objects like crutches. Previously, it never felt comfortable when I used a traditional keyboard to do this for my left arm, but with this keyboard, it does. Now, with both arms/shoulders braced, I find that it is much easier and even automatic to keep my back straight and my head up. It has greatly eased not just arm and hand strain, but back, shoulders and neck strain as well. In addition, I make a point to take my hands completely off the keyboard and mouse when reading, vs. keyboarding, and the pillows give me a comfortable place to elevate my hands, on the top of the pillow where it extends from beneath my underarm.

I rate this product as follows:
Ease of use: 4 stars (should improve with practice)
Functionality for preventing muscle strain: 5 stars
Comfort of use on wrist: 3 stars
Ease of assembly: 4 stars
Attractiveness of keyboard: 4 stars
text_fidelity_b: KINESIS Freestyle2 Ergonomic Keyboard w/ VIP3 Lifters for Mac (9" Separation)

I was very interested in trying this adapter to see if it really is that much faster. It’s absolutely very fast and has wonderful connection reliability but suffers from a very slow software installation process.

I connected it to a Windows 7 64-bit system and allowed Windows to search for a driver. When that failed (as I assumed it would since this is a new product) I put in the installation CD and started the installer. The process took a surprisingly long time just to install and load the driver, to the point that I considered rebooting the box and starting over. It did finish though and then was ready to connect.

It connected without effort to our 5GHz network and immediately was able to serve up content. Everything seemed to be faster but we were not sure - until my teenage son connected to a Minecraft server and started playing. In addition to a lag-free connection he noticed about a 20% gain in frame rates sustained.

So far I can’t find anything beyond the clunky install that stands out as a negative. This is a fast adapter and it worth the one-time install time if you want fast, reliable connections and have a router that can handle the 802.11ac standard.

HP 410 Slim Bluetooth Mouse - Bluetooth 5.0, Swift Pair, Blue optical sensor, adjustable up to 1600 DPI tracking, Portable, sleek for Wins PC, Laptop, Notebook, Mac, Work with Chromebook (4M0X5AA#ABL) Since 2010, every time I’ve bought a new laptop, I’ve bought a new wireless mouse. I don’t like using the one on the laptop as it is too awkward and clunky for me.

The mice I prefer – Logitech. The most recent one I got was: Logitech M317 – Amazon code B08L8SRJRR; white with purple/pink side grip, flowers on top. Though I did get it from Staples (the branding is shortened to Logi).

To me, the brand doesn’t matter – I do try to keep my equipment the same, but the Logitech ones have never let me down. They’re also better shaped for my hand, though the ones of the last decade are smaller, which I LOVE. Last year when I got a new laptop for my birthday, I got the new little Logi listed above.

I saw another HP mouse on here, the HP 930 Creator, and though that would be awesome. It wasn’t. I was quite disappointed. Not that I didn’t like my Logi, I though the HP would be a bit better. And, the 930 was over $67. Many problems, but the main one – size. Far too big for me in height and width.

I saw this and thought it might be better than the 930 – was certainly simpler. I love the FLAT design. It’s about half the height of my Logi.

This, like the 930 has a width problem, thus small hands and those with dexterity issues will have some problems “getting a grip”.

Another issue with this – you need BLUETOOTH capabilities.

Function?

Connection: After turning on my computer’s BLUETOOTH, the mouse connected in under 5 minutes

Sound: A bit quieter than my Logi, as well as the 930 Creator

Scroll: A bit slower than the Logi, definitely slower than the 930

Battery Replacement: Logi – on the bottom, like usual; 930 (rechargeable through USB). This? The battery is on the TOP. You have to remove the top black plate to put the battery in. This is the feature I dislike the most considering how THIN the plastic piece is. Depending on the amount of force used – it could easily get broken.

Currently priced at $39.76, this is definitely a bit overpriced. I am not fond of it, and definitely wouldn’t get a replacement.

UPDATE: As of 3/26, the mouse keeps losing Bluetooth connectivity sometimes in as little as 15 minutes of non-use. I don't know if this is normal with the Bluetooth mouse, but it is definitely annoying especially when I have to reconnect.
text_fidelity_b: HP 410 Slim Bluetooth Mouse - Bluetooth 5.0, Swift Pair, Blue optical sensor, adjustable up to 1600 DPI tracking, Portable, sleek for Wins PC, Laptop, Notebook, Mac, Work with Chromebook (4M0X5AA#ABL)

TBMAX Portable Reading Light Gooseneck Tube Dimmable Desk Lamp with Adjusted Clip-On Stand, Touch-Sensitive Switch, Adapter, and 3 Brightness Levels, 2.5W - White I received this is a free review sample. For the price this is a bargain, but there are two things that kept me from giving it five stars. First is this does not use a standard micro USB style cable for charging. That means that unless you can find an easy source of cables with USB A on one end and the barrel connector this one has on the other, you are stuck with a three foot limitation of cable length. I have USB micro cables that are double that, and would have made this light all the more useful. Also, since I am using this as a music stand light if I misplace it for a gig I am out of luck because I do not own a similar charging cable (although I always have spare USB micro cables in my gig bag.) If you intend to use this as a fixed table lamp the cable issue will not be the problem for you that it is for me.

Second, the gooseneck is sensitive. If I bump a music stand with this light clamped to the shelf it will move far out of place. It's not stiff enough to hold if you do plan to use it with a music stand. For tables, bed stands, etc. it should work fine, though.

Here are some of the strengths: the lowest setting of illumination is perfect for stage use or if you want to read in bed without waking your partner up. At the highest setting it is definitely bright when lose in (about 1.5 meters), and - as Goldilocks said - the medium setting is just right.

Another feature is untethered to the charger this will operate for three hours at the brightest setting and half more than double that at the lowest. That means that if you are camping, on stage (or in front of a lectern) without a power source nearby you can still use it.

Finally, the included wall wart has a 2 Amp port for phones and tablets, as well as a 500mA port for charging this light. That is handy and all the more reason why the cable style for this lamp is a frustration - it could have easily been a five star product, and especially at the going price.
text_fidelity_b: TBMAX Portable Reading Light Gooseneck Tube Dimmable Desk Lamp with Adjusted Clip-On Stand, Touch-Sensitive Switch, Adapter, and 3 Brightness Levels, 2.5W - White

NETGEAR Orbi Whole Home Tri-Band Mesh WiFi 6 System (RBK653) Router with 2 Satellite Extenders, Coverage Up to 6,000 Square Feet, 40 Devices, AX3000 (Up to 3Gbps) There is nothing more frustrating than having dead zones in your own home where you have poor connectivity. I got this router in anticipation of my two young girls growing into teenagers. The internet is an integral part of their educational and social life, so it's imperative to have good coverage throughout the house to reduce family stress.

The system consists of a router and two satellite signal boosters that you can use to ensure great internet throughout your home. As you can see from the pictures, the router has two gigabit ethernet ports. The satellites have a power plug and a sync button.

Every component is highly compact at 4.1 by 4.1 by 2.7 inches. There is also an app that allows you to have convenient control options on your phone. You also receive a 2 meter ethernet cable and three power adapters for the router and satellites.

The router and satellites are easy to hook up and sync. You can place them strategically throughout your home to ensure you get great internet coverage everywhere. I always make everyone in my family use their wi-fi on their phone rather than a data plan, so by reducing poor connectivity zones this router will definitely be a long term savings. I also like the compact size and design of all three elements. This is a great system for getting the most out of your internet.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR Orbi Whole Home Tri-Band Mesh WiFi 6 System (RBK653) Router with 2 Satellite Extenders, Coverage Up to 6,000 Square Feet, 40 Devices, AX3000 (Up to 3Gbps)
